<p class="intro">
  A diamond's price reflects more than its size. This project uses the
  built-in <code>diamonds</code> dataset from ggplot2 to explore how carat
  relates to price—and whether cut quality changes the picture.
</p>

## Carat and price

Each point represents one diamond. Color indicates its cut quality, and
transparency makes dense regions easier to see.

::: {.plot-wrap}
```{r}
#| label: fig-carat-price
#| fig-cap: "Price rises with carat, with substantial variation at every size."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of price against carat for all 53,940 diamonds. Points are colored by cut quality and transparent where they overlap."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price, color = cut)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Cut quality") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 5, by = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Price (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#173b3a"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What stands out

Price generally climbs as carat increases, but diamonds of similar weight can
still have very different prices. The colored bands overlap considerably, so
cut alone does not explain the price pattern. Transparency helps reveal the
concentration of smaller, lower-priced stones without hiding less common
larger diamonds.
:::

<p class="project-note">
  Dataset: ggplot2's built-in <code>diamonds</code> data ·
  53,940 observations plotted · No sampling
</p>
